title: At RAND, Paul Baran designed a network that would survive a nuclear attack, and his idea made ARPANET possible

trailer.text: Paul Baran, an electrical engineer born to a Jewish family in Grodno, was one of the inventors of packet switching, the basis of data communication in computer networks around the world.
At RAND he examined AT&T’s telephone network and concluded that a small number of well-placed bombs could disrupt communications throughout the country.
His solution was a distributed, digital network, in which messages are broken into message blocks that are sent separately and reassembled at the destination.
According to EBSCO, AT&T insisted that the idea was unworkable.

According to an AI-generated summary on the Britannica website, which carries a warning that it may contain errors, ARPA rediscovered the idea and it became the key concept that made ARPANET possible.

glance.value: Paul Baran, an electrical engineer from a Jewish family

glance.label: What
glance.value: A digital distributed network and packet switching

paragraphs.text: Paul Baran was born on April 29, 1926, in Grodno, Poland, now in Belarus.
On May 11, 1928, the family moved to the United States and settled in Boston.
In Philadelphia, his father, Morris Baran, opened a grocery store.
In 1949 Baran completed a degree in electrical engineering at Drexel.
He joined the Eckert-Mauchly company and worked on UNIVAC models, the first brand of commercial computers in the United States.
In 1955 he moved to Los Angeles and worked at Hughes Aircraft on radar data processing systems.
Through night classes at UCLA he received a master’s degree in engineering in 1959.
According to his advisor, he was the only student who went to the Patent Office to check whether his thesis work could be patented.

stations.title: A network that collapses from a few bombs

paragraphs.text: Baran left Hughes and joined RAND’s computer science department.
There he became interested in the survivability of communications systems in the event of a nuclear attack.
He examined AT&T’s telephone network and concluded that it was vulnerable: a small number of well-placed bombs could disrupt communications throughout the country.
The reason was the network’s centralized design.
Baran wanted to prevent a nuclear holocaust, not for money or fame, but out of personal anxiety.
He recounted that he first proposed relaying teletype signals from one AM broadcast station to another, building on an idea by Frank Collbohm, the president of RAND.
According to the history, the Air Force replied that the proposal might suit the President, but communicating with forces in the field required a system with much greater capacity.
Baran was influenced by the principle that the human brain can recover lost functions by bypassing a dysfunctional area.
He considered breaking large messages into message blocks, each sent separately and reassembled at the destination.
He did not use the word “packets” but rather “blocks” or “message-blocks.”
Baran recounted that analog signals deteriorate rapidly when they pass through many links in tandem, and therefore concluded that all communications would have to be digital.
In the system he described, each node attempts to get rid of its messages, and if the preferred route is busy or destroyed, it chooses an alternate route (“hot potato”).
According to Baran, a critical mass of the network was reached at about 15–20 nodes in width, with a redundancy of about three times the minimum number of links.
A 1962 RAND paper examines a high-speed digital data transmission network, composed of unreliable links, that nevertheless has some desired level of reliability and survivability.
Baran’s work was published in a series of RAND studies between 1960 and 1962.
In November 1962 Baran presented a paper titled On Distributed Communications Networks.
In August 1964 RAND published his multivolume study, “On Distributed Communications.”
His ideas were considered radical at the time, and met resistance from proponents of the circuit switching that was conventional in the telephone network.
Baran recounted that he conducted about forty or more briefings around the country, in government and at major research organizations.
According to EBSCO, he first approached AT&T, but decision makers there insisted that the idea was unworkable, despite repeated approaches.
According to Baran, AT&T, which held the monopoly on telecommunications, was among the most negative parties.
According to AP, the idea was so advanced for its time that private companies passed on it.
Baran recounted that in 1965 a formal RAND recommendation to implement his plan was submitted to the Air Force.
According to Baran, the Department of Defense ruled that the Defense Communications Agency, not the Air Force, should build the system.
Baran recommended shelving the project, arguing that it was better to wait for the right group to manage its creation.
An interview abstract at the Charles Babbage Institute notes his decision not to implement the network in 1966.
In a 1967 document Baran listed the limitations of existing systems: vulnerability, limited secrecy, high error rate, delay and rising cost.

According to an AI-generated summary on the Britannica website, which carries a warning that it may contain errors, the military initially ignored the idea, but ARPA rediscovered it and it became the key concept that made ARPANET possible.
According to EBSCO, the development of ARPANET incorporated the distributed network idea and Baran’s packet-switching method.
According to the Lemelson Program, Lawrence Roberts adopted Baran’s distributed network and packet-switching schemes, and Baran was an informal consultant to the project.
At first ARPANET connected only four nodes.
It was heterogeneous: its computers did not need to be compatible with one another.
In Britain, Donald Davies explored similar ideas in the mid-1960s and gave the method the name “packet switching.”
According to RAND, Davies developed a similar system independently, and it was his term that was eventually adopted.
Baran was glad to acknowledge that Davies arrived at the same idea independently.

stations.title: After RAND: the future, modems and companies

paragraphs.text: In 1966 Baran presented a paper on the future of marketing to the American Marketing Association.
According to his son, Baran wrote in 1966 that by the year 2000 people would be using online networks for shopping and news.
In 1968 he left RAND to help found the Institute for the Future, together with RAND colleagues.
In 1972 he founded CableData to explore moving data on cable television networks.
The Telebit TrailBlazer modem achieved data rates of about 18 kilobits per second, while contemporary modems delivered 2400 bits per second.
Baran founded Metricom, which led to the Ricochet system.
According to the National Academy of Engineering memorial tribute, in 1986, and it was cofounded

stations.title: Recognition, and what was said of him

paragraphs.text: In 1990 Baran received the IEEE Alexander Graham Bell Medal.
In 2007 he was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.
President George Bush awarded him the National Medal of Technology.
In 2009 the UCLA school of engineering gave him the Alumnus of the Year Award, its highest honor.
RAND President James Thomson said that the world is better for the technologies Baran invented and developed, and for his concern with appropriate public policy.
Vint Cerf said that Baran was not afraid to go in directions counter to what everyone else thought was the right or only thing to do.
According to the National Academy of Engineering memorial tribute, Baran was modest, always minimized his own part and gave much to others.
He said that if you are not careful, you can convince yourself that you did the most important part.
According to EBSCO, he always stressed that the modern Internet was the result of the work of hundreds of people, not of one or two innovations.
According to James Pelkey, Baran believed that innovation was a team effort.
Evelyn, his wife since 1955, died in 2007.
Baran died in 2011 at his home in Palo Alto, of complications from lung cancer.
According to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), Paul Baran was among the 2007 laureates of the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
According to the Computer History Museum, Paul Baran passed away on March 26, 2011.

stations.title: Who invented it, and what was missed

paragraphs.text: It was Davies's work, not Baran's, that first drew the attention of the ARPANET developers.
The number of inventors is also disputed: there were two, and according to ARRL, three.
The presentation of Leonard Kleinrock's early work as the source of the idea of packet switching is disputed among other Internet pioneers.
According to his son, it took decades for the social and commercial possibilities of the technology to become clear, and Baran missed out on much of the money and glory.

disagreements.question: In what year did Baran join RAND?

versions.says: According to the National Academy of Engineering memorial tribute, in 1960

disagreements.question: How many volumes did the On Distributed Communications series comprise?

versions.says: According to History of Computer Communications, Volumes I through XI
According to the Computer History Museum, 13 volumes
According to the interview abstract at the Charles Babbage Institute, eleven volumes

disagreements.question: When was the technology adopted to create ARPANET?

versions.says: According to ARRL, MIT and DARPA adopted the technology in 1968
According to AP, in 1969 the Department of Defense used it in creating ARPANET
According to EBSCO, development of ARPANET began in 1967

disagreements.question: How many companies did Baran found?

versions.says: According to UCLA, seven start-up companies, five of which went public
According to the National Academy of Engineering memorial tribute, ten companies that he founded or cofounded
According to the Lemelson Program, six companies in Silicon Valley

disagreements.question: Was Baran one of two or one of three inventors of packet switching?

versions.says: According to ARRL, one of three, along with Donald Davies and Leonard Kleinrock

claims.text: ב-2009 העניק בית הספר להנדסה של UCLA לברן את פרס בוגר השנה, ההוקרה הגבוהה ביותר שלו.
claims.quote: In 2009, the UCLA Henry Samueli School of Engineering and Applied Science awarded Baran with the Alumnus of the Year Award, the school’s highest honor.

claims.text: נשיא RAND ג'יימס תומסון אמר שהעולם טוב יותר בזכות הטכנולוגיות שברן המציא ופיתח ובזכות דאגתו למדיניות ציבורית הולמת.
claims.quote: Our world is a better place for the technologies Paul Baran invented and developed, and also because of his consistent concern with appropriate public policies for their use,

claims.text: וינט סרף אמר שברן לא חשש ללכת בכיוונים הנוגדים את מה שכולם חשבו שהוא הדבר הנכון או היחיד.
claims.quote: Paul wasn’t afraid to go in directions counter to what everyone else thought was the right or only thing to do

claims.text: ברן היה צנוע ותמיד הקטין את חלקו שלו ונתן הרבה לאחרים.
claims.quote: Ever modest, Baran never failed to minimize his own credit and gave much to others.

claims.text: ברן אמר שאם לא נזהרים אפשר לשכנע את עצמך שעשית את החלק החשוב ביותר.
claims.quote: If you are not careful you can con yourself into believing that you did the most important part.

claims.text: לפי EBSCO, ברן הדגיש תמיד שהאינטרנט המודרני הוא תוצאה של עבודת מאות אנשים ולא של חידוש אחד או שניים.
claims.quote: Baran was always quick to point out that the modern Internet was the result of not one or two innovations but the hard work of hundreds of people

claims.text: לפי ג'יימס פלקי, ברן האמין שהחדשנות היא מאמץ צוותי.
claims.quote: and believed that the act of innovation was a team effort

claims.text: אשתו של ברן מאז 1955, אוולין, מתה ב-2007.
claims.quote: Baran’s wife since 1955, Evelyn, died in 2007.

claims.text: לפי ARRL, ברן מת ב-27 במרץ בביתו בפאלו אלטו.
claims.quote: died March 27 at his home in Palo Alto, California.

claims.text: לפי EBSCO, ברן מת ב-26 במרץ 2011 מסיבוכי סרטן ריאות.
claims.quote: He died on March 26, 2011, of complications from lung cancer.

claims.text: לפי ARRL, ברן היה אחד משלושה ממציאי הרשתות מבוססות המנות, יחד עם דונלד דייויס ולאונרד קליינרוק.
claims.quote: Baran was one of the three inventors of packet-switched networks, along with Donald Davies and Leonard Kleinrock.

claims.text: לפי בנו, חלפו עשורים עד שהאפשרויות החברתיות והמסחריות של הטכנולוגיה התבהרו, וברן החמיץ חלק גדול מהכסף והתהילה.
claims.quote: It would be decades before the social and commercial possibilities of the technology would become clear, and Baran would miss out on a lot of the money and glory that came with it

claims.text: לפי ההספד של האקדמיה הלאומית להנדסה, ברן הצטרף ל-RAND ב-1960.
claims.quote: Baran joined the RAND Corporation in 1960, two years after the invention of the integrated circuit.

claims.text: תקציר הראיון במכון צ'רלס באבאג' מתאר את כתיבתו והפצתו של חיבור בן אחד-עשר כרכים.
claims.quote: the writing and distribution of his eleven-volume work

claims.text: לפי ARRL, ב-1968 אימצו MIT ו-DARPA את הטכנולוגיה כדי ליצור את ARPANET.
claims.quote: In 1968, the technology was adopted by MIT and the DARPA -- the Department of Defense’s research agency -- to create what became the Advanced Research Projects Agency Network

claims.text: לפי דיווח AP, ב-1969 הפכה הטכנולוגיה לרעיון שמשרד ההגנה השתמש בו ביצירת ארפנט.
claims.quote: In 1969 the technology became a concept the Department of Defense used in creating the Arpanet, the precursor to the Internet

claims.text: לפי UCLA, ברן הקים שבע חברות סטארט-אפ, חמש מהן הונפקו.
claims.quote: In all, he founded seven start-up companies, five of which went public.

claims.text: לפי ההספד של ה-NAE, ברן הקים או הקים במשותף עשר חברות לאורך השנים.
claims.quote: That Baran resonated strongly with this idea is evident from the 10 companies that he founded or cofounded over the years.

claims.text: לפי מעבדת למלסון, ברן הקים שש חברות בעמק הסיליקון.
claims.quote: He founded six companies in Silicon Valley including Cable Data Associates, established in Menlo Park in 1974.

claims.text: לפי משרד הפטנטים והסימנים המסחריים של ארה"ב (USPTO), פול ברן נמנה עם עטורי מדליית הטכנולוגיה והחדשנות הלאומית לשנת 2007.
claims.quote: 2007 Laureates- National Medal of Technology and Innovation

claims.text: לפי מוזיאון ההיסטוריה של המחשוב, פול ברן הלך לעולמו ב-26 במרץ 2011.
claims.quote: passed away on March 26, 2011

claims.text: פול ברן, מהנדס חשמל שנולד למשפחה יהודית בגרודנו, היה אחד מממציאי מיתוג המנות, הבסיס לתקשורת הנתונים ברשתות מחשבים בעולם.
claims.quote: Paul Baran invented the field of packet switching networks while conducting research at the historic RAND organization

claims.text: פול ברן, מהנדס חשמל שנולד למשפחה יהודית בגרודנו, היה אחד מממציאי מיתוג המנות, הבסיס לתקשורת הנתונים ברשתות מחשבים בעולם.
claims.quote: Paul Baran was born in Grodno, Poland, in 1926.

claims.text: מה: רשת מבוזרת דיגיטלית ומיתוג מנות
claims.quote: Baran's packet switching ideas served as a foundation upon which others later built the ARPANET.

claims.text: ברן שמח להודות שדייויס הגיע לאותו רעיון באופן עצמאי.
claims.quote: He was an honest guy, and I'm sure it was done independently.

claims.text: ברן שמח להודות שדייויס הגיע לאותו רעיון באופן עצמאי.
claims.quote: Davies came along later and independently came up with much of the same stuff.

claims.text: ברן הקים את Metricom, שהובילה למערכת Ricochet.
claims.quote: In 1986, Baran cofounded Metricom, Inc.

claims.text: ברן הקים את Metricom, שהובילה למערכת Ricochet.
claims.quote: which led to the Ricochet wireless data communications system

claims.text: דווקא עבודתו של דייויס, ולא של ברן, משכה תחילה את תשומת לבם של מפתחי ARPANET.
claims.quote: Scantlebury took Roberts aside after hearing his talk, and told him all about something called packet-switching.

claims.text: דווקא עבודתו של דייויס, ולא של ברן, משכה תחילה את תשומת לבם של מפתחי ARPANET.
claims.quote: Roberts and Taylor seem never to have taken notice of them.

claims.text: גם מספר הממציאים שנוי במחלוקת: הם היו שניים, ולפי ARRL שלושה.
claims.quote: Baran was one of the three inventors of packet-switched networks, along with Donald Davies and Leonard Kleinrock.

claims.text: גם מספר הממציאים שנוי במחלוקת: הם היו שניים, ולפי ARRL שלושה.
claims.quote: The packet switching concept was first invented by Paul Baran in the early 1960’s, and then independently a few years later by Donald Davies.

claims.text: ההצגה של עבודתו המוקדמת של לאונרד קליינרוק כמקור הרעיון של מיתוג מנות שנויה במחלוקת בין חלוצי אינטרנט אחרים.
claims.quote: Therefore, we must conclude that Kleinrock's claim to precedence for this concept is not supported by the evidence.

claims.text: אחד משני ממציאים עצמאיים
claims.quote: The packet switching concept was first invented by Paul Baran in the early 1960’s, and then independently a few years later by Donald Davies.
